Haruki

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two chords of a circle and two more circles mark out two equal lengths on one chord.
How to play: Drag any named point, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, the equal lengths, or the angle hint.
Look for the math

Drag P around the circle and the picture changes completely, yet two lengths marked in green stay equal. Hiroshi Haruki's lemma explains why, and the same idea also proves the Butterfly theorem.

The construction

All five named points lie on one circle. The chords AB and CD are fixed while P slides around the circle. Let Q be where PC crosses AB and R where PD crosses AB. The circle through P, Q, D crosses AB again at E; the circle through P, R, C crosses AB again at F. The applet draws all of these, and the two green pieces of AB are BE and AF.

The equal lengths

Apply the intersecting chords theorem to the chords PD and AE inside the large circle and inside the circle PQD. Both give the same product: PR·RD = AR·RB and PR·RD = QR·RE. Since RE = RB + BE and AR = AQ + QR, we get QR·BE = AQ·RB. The circle PRC gives the same expression for AF, so BE = AF = AQ·RB / QR. This is exactly what the page states, and the check confirms it on thousands of figures.

Why E and F stay put

In the circle PQD, the angles ∠QPD and ∠QED stand on the same chord QD, so they are equal inscribed angles. The angle at P changes as P moves, but ∠QPD = ∠CPD is fixed by the fixed chord CD, so the angle ∠AED is fixed too. A fixed angle from the fixed line AD cuts AB at one fixed point E; the same argument fixes F. That is why BE and AF do not depend on where P sits on the circle. The hint box marks the equal angles at F, P and E.

What the checks found

The logic test rebuilds the whole figure a second way, directly from the applet's bytecode, and compares every point on more than two thousand generated configurations, including chords that are almost horizontal. It also sweeps P all the way round fixed chords: E and F never move. One faithful quirk remains: the old applet decides which intersection is E or F by a one-unit rule, so when the two crossings are closer than a unit apart it can pick the wrong one. The theorem is still true; only the drawing is ambiguous there.

The live page now uses a GeoGebra figure instead of the Java applet. The archived 2010 page shows the original Haruki applet embedded with the same wording and the names, statement and hint switches.

Try dragging P past C or D: E and F stay where they are, and the two green lengths keep their size.
